tweets.text:
Chatted with a friend who leads security at a public company following the GPT Sol incident. some interesting takeaways.. 

How do you manage security for effectively infinite agents when identity and access management was designed for a finite number of employees?

One employee can now spin up hundreds of agents. Those agents can spawn more agents.

Traditionally, each employee has an identity, a role, permissions, and a lifecycle.

Do agents inherit the spawning employee’s permissions? What’s their lifecycle - a task, a ticket, a week? Do child agents inherit the same permissions? How do you audit all of this?

Using a Chinese-trained LLM doesn’t mean they get your data. 

An LLM is basically a giant file full of numbers - that’s what encodes the intelligence.

Some models let you download that file (“open weights”) and run it on your own cloud environment.

The model trainer is out of the picture now. Your data stays wherever you’re running it.

tweets.text:
Very good post from the Head of Economics at Anthropic. They’re finding that jobs have been less negatively impacted by AI than expected, as we continue to see time and time again in the data.

The reason for this is that AI - at least so far - still requires people to operate to produce value in most cases. Most jobs can’t be fully automated with AI, only certain tasks in those jobs. And when you automate specific tasks, you actually can get even more output from those jobs, raising the demand (or at least maintaining it) in many cases.

“So far, AI is both skill-biased and labor-augmenting. It complements domain expertise. It relies on humans in the loop to direct and evaluate the most complex work. And it rewards AI proficiency. Model capabilities are improving fast, but remain stubbornly jagged. To fill in the pockets of the jagged frontier, expert oversight is needed to steer incredibly capable AI systems, and to recover when they falter.”

I suspect that we continue to see this in a number of critical areas of work. It’s clearly happening in software engineering, where software produced is being multiplied, all of which still requires developers to manage the work agents are doing. Software engineers are needed in a wide variety of industries now and companies of all sizes can now light up software projects that would have been impractical before.

But there will be plenty of other domains of work where demand remains strong in a world where agents can accelerate the output of that job. Jevons paradox is alive and well.

Arthur Hayes @CryptoHayes 为BitMEX即将关停发声谢幕：

感谢我的合伙人、BitMEX的员工们，以及最重要的——我们的客户们。

这是一段精彩的旅程。我们一起做了件特别的事。我为自己们所创造的一切感到无比自豪，也为我们能以自己的方式、负责任地关闭而骄傲。

去他的TradFi，去他的银行，中本聪永存！

除了被美国监管，BitMEX最出名的一件事大概就是312那次「拔网线」了

2020年3月12日下午六点半开始，比特币为首的加密货币突然开始大跳水⚠️📉所有人猝不及防。

行情软件的报价不断闪动，比特币价格从7000美元开始无抵抗下跌，一路击碎所有人的侥幸。24小时内暴跌近50%。而当时作为空单持仓量最大的交易平台BitMEX在13日上午将平台交易功能暂停，俗称「拔网线」。

从某种角度看，这拯救了比特币。在无抵抗下跌的过程中，BitMEX上已经没有买单，如果不拔网线，比特币在该平台价格将归零。

而当时其他交易平台也是人仰马翻，套利搬砖机器人早已超过其工作范围，各平台间比特币价差高达1000美元。

BitMEX对整个加密市场的发展可以说产生了举足轻重的影响的。作为首个推出并成功普及永续合约的加密交易平台，它几乎重塑了加密衍生品市场，也深刻影响了此后整个行业的发展。

不知道圈内老人看到这条新闻是什么感想...🥲🥲

2020年，美国司法部和美国商品期货交易委员会（CFTC）以违反《银行保密法》、未建立有效反洗钱体系等指控起诉Hayes等联创，认为BitMEX非法向美国用户提供服务。

此后，BitMEX市场份额也在Binance、OKX等竞争对手崛起过程中持续萎缩，行业龙头地位逐渐被取代。

2025年2月，市场曾传出其寻求出售的消息，但未公布后续进展。

这篇2021年《名利场》发布的万字长文记录了这家「期货合约之王」早期的崛起与转折，分享给大家：https://t.co/pKgwNNa5SN

💬CZ @cz_binance  发文致敬🫡Arthur Hayes @CryptoHayes  ：很遗憾看到BitMEX @BitMEX 关闭，其早在2014年首创百倍加密合约

7 月 23 日，Binance @cz_binance  创始人 CZ 发文致敬 BitMEX 创始人 Arthur Hayes。很遗憾看到 BitMEX 关闭。一些想法：

BitMEX 早在 2014 年就率先推出了 100 倍加密货币交易。交割期货在此之前就已经存在，使得周五的交易异常火爆。BitMEX 只接受比特币充值，只支持一条链，每天只能提现一次，而且必须通过多重签名钱包。这些看似不便的限制反而让他们免遭黑客攻击。

在经历了 18 个月的抗争后，四位创始人最终在审判前一个月承认违反了《银行保密法》(BSA)。他们每人被罚款 1000 万美元，并被软禁在家。没有人因此入狱。然而，他们的业务最终没能挺过拜登政府发起的「加密货币战争」。

最后，BitMEX 的清算过程看起来井然有序，用户可以提取他们的资产。向 Arthur Hayes 致敬。

This is one of the hardest edges of the economic singularity. 

Full framework in the article I wrote this week: https://t.co/t2ufisdHPI

People can't conceive of how fast this is coming.

Look at just the last few years of AI. It's moved faster than we can legislate, faster than we can debate, faster than any institution was built to handle. And that's the slow part. It only accelerates from here.

That's a huge elephant in the room. Shifts this big would normally go through a democratic process. People debate it, it works its way through… But that takes decades. And we don't have decades.

When the ground moves this fast and process can't keep up, governments reach for whatever knob they have. And control tends to get more centralised, not because anyone wants it, but because the democratic process simply isn't fast enough to catch what's coming.

This is the part of the Economic Singularity nobody wants to look at. It isn't just markets and machines moving to a speed we can't follow. It's our whole system of governing arriving too late.

It is the ideal of the data production and training regime, and it is bounded by human data and preference.

We are approaching AGI not as a threshold but as a limit.

Superintelligence, or ASI, is something else. General intelligence is table stakes. ASI learns from its own experiences and has potentially unbounded capability.

Nobody has yet discovered a learner capable of meeting all of the conditions for ASI. Current RL cannot correctly assign credit to individual tokens for reward, so it is distributed across massive numbers of rollouts— not exactly a single agent learning from experience.

I do believe this is possible, and like the math conjectures currently being demolished may just be a matter of time and compute.
